o: Distinguish copper, fibre-optic and wireless connections.
Explain suitable advantages and drawbacks for each.
Describe why wireless communication needs protection.
c: Wired copper connections carry electrical signals and are affordable, but have speed/distance limits.
Fibre carries pulses of light, supporting high rates and long distances; installation can be more costly.
Wi-Fi uses radio waves so devices can move without cables, but connections may experience interference and interception.
Use the scenario: high bandwidth, cost, mobility, length of cable, interference and security matter.

m.title: Connecting separate buildings
m.q: A college connects two buildings a long distance apart. Explain why fibre optic may be more suitable than copper. [4 marks]
st: The connection is between buildings over a substantial distance.
Fibre uses light pulses [1] and is suitable for high-speed, longer-distance links [1].
Copper carries electrical signals [1] and has greater limitations on speed/distance for such a link [1].
Two contrasts, each explained in context, make four points.

w: A cafe provides wireless access to customers using phones and tablets. Explain two reasons Wi-Fi is suitable. [4 marks]
Wireless uses radio rather than cables to each device [1], allowing users to move while connected [1]. Devices can join without dedicated physical ports [1], making guest access more flexible [1].
A business handles confidential data over Wi-Fi. Explain two risks and how encryption helps. [4 marks]

Wireless signals can be intercepted by nearby devices [1], creating a confidentiality risk [1]. Encryption scrambles transmitted data [1], so captured content cannot be understood without the key [1].
A hospital must connect fixed machines reliably. Explain one benefit and one drawback of a wired connection. [4 marks]
Wired cables provide a stable link less affected by radio interference [1], improving reliability [1]. The cable restricts device movement [1], reducing flexibility if machines are relocated [1].
wSteps: Choose mobility and ease of connecting many visitors.
Wi-Fi connects by radio [1] and without individual cables [1].
Users can move [1] and join more flexibly [1].
Wireless uses radio rather than cables to each device [1], allowing users to move while connected [1]. Devices can join without dedicated physical ports [1], making guest access more flexible [1].
Signals travel through air [1] and can be captured [1].
Encryption protects readable content [1] using a required key [1].

Wireless signals can be intercepted by nearby devices [1], creating a confidentiality risk [1]. Encryption scrambles transmitted data [1], so captured content cannot be understood without the key [1].
Cables are less exposed to radio interference [1], but tie devices to ports [1].
Connection may be more reliable [1], yet harder to move [1].
Wired cables provide a stable link less affected by radio interference [1], improving reliability [1]. The cable restricts device movement [1], reducing flexibility if machines are relocated [1].

k.q: Compare estimated ideal transfer times for two connection rates using the same file size.
k.code:
fileMb = 120
speedMbps = 60
seconds = fileMb / speedMbps
print(seconds)
p: Add print("Estimate only") after the result.
k.a:
Original output 2 seconds; at 30 Mbps output 4 seconds.

Extended OCR ERL:
fileMb = 120
speedMbps = 30
seconds = fileMb / speedMbps
print(seconds)
print("Estimate only")

Outputs: 4 and Estimate only. This assumes a constant rate.

State one disadvantage of wireless transmission. [1 mark]

Source: Adapted from your Paper 1 revision booklet, 1.3.2.
Interference, interception/security risk or variable signal quality [1].

A research station must connect an outdoor field laboratory to its main building. Explain one advantage and one limitation of using fibre-optic cable for this long link. [4 marks]

Source: Original J277-style question, not an OCR past-paper original.

Fibre carries light-based signals [1] and is well suited to high-speed/long-distance links [1]. Installing fibre can be more costly or difficult [1], increasing the cost/complexity of the research station's connection [1].

Compare copper, fibre and wireless communication for a school. [6 marks]

Source: Original J277-style question, not an OCR past-paper original.

Copper carries electrical signals [1] and is cost-effective for local wired links [1]. Fibre carries light [1] and offers high speed/long distance [1]. Wireless uses radio [1] and offers mobility but may suffer interference/interception [1].
v: A link using a physical cable.
Transmission medium carrying signals as light.
Communication without a connecting cable, often radio.
Scrambling data so unintended recipients cannot read it without the key.
x: A wireless connection always needs a separate cable from every phone to the access point.
r: State one advantage of a mesh topology. [1 mark]
Several routes provide fault tolerance if a link fails [1].
State one purpose of DNS. [2 marks]
It looks up an IP address [1] associated with a requested domain name [1].
State one difference between RAM and ROM, referring to whether each retains data without power. [2 marks]
RAM is volatile: its stored information is lost when power is switched off [1]. ROM is non-volatile: its contents remain stored without power [1].
Two students directly exchange files between laptops. Explain a benefit and a drawback of peer-to-peer networking. [4 marks]
No dedicated server needed [1], reducing cost [1]. The other laptop can be off [1], preventing shared-file access [1].

priorExam.q: A small school's computers all connect to one central switch. Name the topology and explain what may happen if the switch fails. [3 marks]
priorExam.a: Star topology [1]. The switch is the central connection point [1], so if it fails connected devices may be unable to communicate [1].
